items.explanation: To streamline oversight, the NPC established the Data Breach Notification Management System (DBNMS) as the exclusive, mandatory interface for submissions. Physical or ad-hoc email deliveries are procedurally non-compliant.

items.question_text: A registered corporation implements flawless security and experiences absolutely zero incidents, breaches, or blocked attacks all year. What must they file for their ASIR?
options: They are entirely exempt from filing an ASIR for that calendar year.
They must formally submit an ASIR declaring zero incidents via the DBNMS.
They only need to send a brief email to the NPC compliance desk.
They must undergo an expensive physical audit to verify the zero incidents.
items.correct_answer: They must formally submit an ASIR declaring zero incidents via the DBNMS.
items.explanation: The Annual Security Incident Report (ASIR) is a mandatory compliance requirement for registered entities. Even if a company has a perfect record, they must formally file the report to declare zero incidents.

items.question_text: A DPO submits the preliminary 72-hour report but realizes complex forensics will take 10 more days, exceeding the 5-day deadline for the Full Breach Report. What must they do?
options: Wait silently until forensics complete, then submit the massive final report.
Proactively submit a formal written request for an extension before the 5 days expire.
Retract the preliminary notification and entirely restart the 72-hour clock.
Submit the report to the Department of Information and Communications Technology.
items.correct_answer: Proactively submit a formal written request for an extension before the 5 days expire.
items.explanation: NPC Circular 16-03 strictly requires the Full Breach Report within 5 days of the preliminary notice. If impossible, the PIC must formally request an extension from the NPC, detailing the forensic delays, before the deadline lapses.

items.lesson_concept: Extraterritorial application based on data subject residency.
items.question_text: An offshore company with no local branches processes the data of foreign nationals temporarily residing in Manila. Does the Philippine DPA apply to this processing?
options: No, the DPA strictly protects only Philippine citizens.
Yes, the DPA applies to data relating to Philippine residents.
No, offshore companies are immune without local equipment.
Yes, but only if the data is processed on local servers.
items.correct_answer: Yes, the DPA applies to data relating to Philippine residents.
items.explanation: Section 6 extends jurisdiction to acts relating to personal information about Philippine citizens OR residents, regardless of the PIC's offshore status or lack of local equipment.

items.question_text: A corporate intelligence firm sells deep-dive background checks on politicians exclusively to paying subscribers. They claim the journalistic exemption under Section 4. Is this valid?
options: Yes, politicians are public figures exempt from privacy.
No, the processing must be intended for the general public.
Yes, financial intelligence qualifies as protected journalism.
No, because political data is Sensitive Personal Information.
items.correct_answer: No, the processing must be intended for the general public.
items.explanation: The journalistic exemption only applies when processing is exclusively for journalistic purposes intended for the general public, not for private, paywalled commercial intelligence.

items.question_text: A citizen files an FOI request for the addresses of all SSS pensioners, citing the DPA exemption for 'discretionary financial benefits'. Will the DPA protect the pensioners' data?
options: No, all government disbursements are considered discretionary.
Yes, standard SSS pensions are not discretionary benefits.
No, FOI requests automatically override DPA protections.
Yes, but the agency must blur the pensioners' last names.
items.correct_answer: Yes, standard SSS pensions are not discretionary benefits.
items.explanation: Section 4(c) exempts discretionary benefits (like specific grants). Routine, legally mandated benefits like standard pensions remain fully protected by the DPA.

items.question_text: A university conducts exempt medical research. They secretly use the findings to expel students flagged with severe genetic risks. What happens to their DPA exemption?
options: It is maintained because the research was originally lawful.
It is voided because the data directly affected the subjects.
It is maintained because universities hold academic freedom.
It is voided because genetic data cannot be used in research.
items.correct_answer: It is voided because the data directly affected the subjects.
items.explanation: The research exemption is instantly nullified if the processed data is subsequently used to make decisions that directly affect the specific data subjects.

items.lesson_concept: Processing foreign data under foreign laws.
items.question_text: A Philippine BPO processes German citizens' data under GDPR rules. A German citizen sues the BPO before the NPC for administrative DPA fines. How will the NPC respond?
options: The NPC will assert jurisdiction due to the BPO's location.
The NPC will dismiss it, as the data is excluded under Sec 4(g).
The NPC will fine the BPO jointly with EU regulators.
The NPC will apply GDPR standards in a local trial.
items.correct_answer: The NPC will dismiss it, as the data is excluded under Sec 4(g).
items.explanation: Section 4(g) explicitly excludes data originally collected from residents of foreign jurisdictions in accordance with foreign laws, protecting local BPOs from dual compliance.

items.question_text: Company A and B are Joint PICs. Company A's secure server is bypassed due to Company B's leaked admin credentials. A victim sues Company A. Is Company A liable?
options: No, liability rests solely on the party that leaked credentials.
Yes, Joint PICs share solidary liability for the whole system.
No, Company A is protected by demonstrating technical security.
Yes, but Company A is only liable for exactly half the damages.
items.correct_answer: Yes, Joint PICs share solidary liability for the whole system.
items.explanation: Joint Controllers share legal accountability. Data subjects can claim full damages against any joint controller, regardless of whose specific failure caused the breach.

items.question_text: A contracted PIP uses its client's encrypted database to train its own proprietary threat-detection AI without permission. What is the legal implication for the PIP?
options: They remain a PIP but violate their Service Level Agreement.
They unlawfully assume the role of an independent PIC.
They automatically become a Joint Controller with the client.
They are legally exempt under the DPA research provision.
items.correct_answer: They unlawfully assume the role of an independent PIC.
items.explanation: By independently determining a new purpose (AI training) for the personal data, the vendor exceeds their PIP mandate and acts as an unauthorized PIC.

items.question_text: A PIC authorizes its PIP to hire a Sub-PIP for database hosting. The Sub-PIP is hacked. Who is primarily accountable to the data subjects and the NPC?
options: The Sub-PIP, because they committed the technical error.
The PIC, as they retain ultimate statutory accountability.
The primary PIP, because they executed the sub-contract.
All three entities share the exact same level of liability.
items.correct_answer: The PIC, as they retain ultimate statutory accountability.
items.explanation: The PIC is the custodian of the data. Accountability cannot be delegated away; the PIC remains primarily liable to the subjects and must seek civil restitution from the PIPs later.

items.question_text: A hacker leaks the financial ledgers of a registered One Person Corporation (OPC) and a Sole Proprietorship. Which entity can claim Data Subject rights under the DPA?
options: Both entities, as they are owned by single individuals.
Only the Sole Proprietorship, as it is a natural person.
Only the OPC, as it is registered with the government.
Neither entity, as businesses lack personal privacy rights.
items.correct_answer: Only the Sole Proprietorship, as it is a natural person.
items.explanation: An OPC is a juridical entity and cannot be a Data Subject. A Sole Proprietorship is legally inseparable from its human owner, granting them standing as a natural person.

items.question_text: Data subjects petition the NPC to issue an arrest warrant against a grossly negligent CEO after a major breach. Does the NPC have the authority to issue this warrant?
options: Yes, the NPC holds supreme judicial power in privacy cases.
No, only regular trial courts can constitutionally issue warrants.
Yes, provided the Department of Justice explicitly co-signs it.
No, the NPC can only issue warrants for administrative fines.
items.correct_answer: No, only regular trial courts can constitutionally issue warrants.
items.explanation: The NPC is an administrative agency with quasi-judicial powers. The power to issue search or arrest warrants is constitutionally reserved exclusively for regular trial court judges.

items.question_text: A corporation creates a database to track and blacklist union organizers, violating the Labor Code. They obtain signed consent forms from informants. Is this lawful?
options: Yes, explicit consent overrides general processing principles.
No, the objective must not be contrary to law or public policy.
Yes, protecting corporate stability is a Legitimate Interest.
No, blacklists must be maintained strictly in manual files.
items.correct_answer: No, the objective must not be contrary to law or public policy.
items.explanation: Legitimate Purpose requires that the processing objective is lawful. Processing data to facilitate an illegal act (union busting) voids the purpose, rendering it unlawful despite consent.

items.question_text: An app forces users to navigate three confusing sub-menus to decline tracking, while the 'Accept All' button is massive and green. Which principle is primarily violated?
options: The Principle of Data Portability.
The Principle of Fairness and Transparency via dark patterns.
The Principle of Privacy by Default.
The Principle of Legitimate Interest.
items.correct_answer: The Principle of Fairness and Transparency via dark patterns.
items.explanation: NPC Circular 2023-04 mandates Fairness in consent. Using deceptive UI (dark patterns) to manipulate or exhaust a user destroys the 'freely given' requirement of consent.

items.question_text: An employer collects the full medical histories of job applicants' spouses during the initial resume screening 'just in case' they are hired and need insurance. Is this compliant?
options: Yes, proactive corporate planning justifies the collection.
No, collecting SPI for hypothetical future use is disproportionate.
Yes, provided the data is encrypted upon HR receipt.
No, employers are completely banned from collecting medical data.
items.correct_answer: No, collecting SPI for hypothetical future use is disproportionate.
items.explanation: Proportionality demands data minimization. Collecting highly sensitive data prematurely for a scenario that may never happen is excessive and violates the principle.

items.question_text: A development team launches a healthcare app without encryption, planning to implement security patches six months later. Which core accountability concept is violated?
options: The Principle of Data Portability.
Privacy by Design, requiring embedded security from the start.
The Doctrine of Legitimate Interest.
The Principle of Active Transparency.
items.correct_answer: Privacy by Design, requiring embedded security from the start.
items.explanation: Accountability requires proactive engineering. Privacy by Design mandates that data protection measures be integrated into the system architecture from day one, not bolted on later.

items.question_text: A telecom provider forces subscribers to agree to a third-party marketing data-sharing clause; otherwise, they cannot activate their cellular service. Why is this consent invalid?
options: Marketing data belongs exclusively to the national government.
Bundling essential services with unnecessary processing is coercive.
The service contract was not notarized by a legal officer.
It is valid because the user voluntarily purchased the SIM card.
items.correct_answer: Bundling essential services with unnecessary processing is coercive.
items.explanation: Consent must be granular and freely given. Tying the provision of an essential service to the mandatory acceptance of unrelated, intrusive processing destroys genuine choice.

items.question_text: A former customer demands the absolute erasure of their tax invoices under the DPA. The business refuses, citing BIR rules requiring a 10-year retention. Who is legally correct?
options: The customer, because the DPA supersedes the internal Tax Code.
The business, because statutory mandates override the Right to Erasure.
The customer, provided they pay an early deletion penalty fee.
The business, but they must transfer the invoices to the NPC.
items.correct_answer: The business, because statutory mandates override the Right to Erasure.
items.explanation: Data subject rights are not absolute. A PIC must lawfully refuse an erasure request if the retention is strictly required to comply with other statutory laws, like BIR regulations.

items.question_text: An executive suspended for harassment invokes the Right to Access to demand the unredacted witness statements of their accusers. Must the DPO comply immediately?
options: Yes, the Right to Access guarantees full visibility into all data.
No, access must be balanced against the safety of whistleblowers.
Yes, but only if the executive pays a corporate administrative fee.
No, HR investigation files are classified as Public Domain data.
items.correct_answer: No, access must be balanced against the safety of whistleblowers.
items.explanation: The Right to Access cannot be weaponized to expose vulnerable third parties. The DPO must balance rights, typically by withholding or heavily redacting whistleblower identities.

items.question_text: A user objects to a bank's promotional emails. The bank claims 'Legitimate Interest' overrides the objection because marketing sustains the business. Is the defense valid?
options: Yes, corporate financial survival is a compelling legitimate ground.
No, the right to object to direct marketing is completely absolute.
Yes, provided the bank offers an opt-out link in the next email.
No, but the bank can legally switch to targeted SMS promotions.
items.correct_answer: No, the right to object to direct marketing is completely absolute.
items.explanation: Unlike standard processing where a balancing test applies, objection to direct marketing (and profiling for it) is absolute. The PIC must cease processing immediately.

items.lesson_concept: Strict civil law definitions of heirs.
items.question_text: A legally annulled ex-spouse discovers a hospital leaked their deceased former partner's records. Can the ex-spouse invoke Section 17 to claim damages?
options: Yes, any former immediate family member can invoke transmissibility.
No, Section 17 strictly limits standing to lawful heirs and assigns.
Yes, provided the ex-spouse proves severe emotional distress.
No, the Right to Damages permanently expires upon physical death.
items.correct_answer: No, Section 17 strictly limits standing to lawful heirs and assigns.
items.explanation: Transmissibility relies on strict civil law. A legally annulled ex-spouse is not a 'lawful heir' and therefore lacks the locus standi to invoke the DPA rights of the deceased.

items.question_text: A platform complies with a Data Portability request by sending a 500-page flattened, image-based PDF of the user's data. Has the platform fulfilled the legal requirement?
options: Yes, a PDF document legally qualifies as an electronic format.
No, the law requires a structured, machine-readable format like CSV.
Yes, provided the PDF file is securely encrypted with a password.
No, they must establish a direct API connection to a competitor.
items.correct_answer: No, the law requires a structured, machine-readable format like CSV.
items.explanation: Data Portability aims to prevent vendor lock-in. A flattened PDF actively defeats interoperability and violates the requirement for a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format.

items.question_text: A blog publishes court transcripts of a politician who was accused of graft but completely acquitted 10 years ago. How does the DPA classify this data?
options: General Personal Information, as the individual was proven innocent.
Sensitive Personal Information, as it relates to an alleged offense.
Public Domain Information, because the trial ended over 5 years ago.
Privileged Information, because the documents came from a court.
items.correct_answer: Sensitive Personal Information, as it relates to an alleged offense.
items.explanation: Section 3(l) protects individuals by classifying any data regarding a proceeding for an offense—whether committed or merely alleged—as SPI, regardless of an eventual acquittal.

items.question_text: A security log requires a Corporate Employee ID Number and a Philippine Passport Number. Under Section 3(l), how are these strictly classified?
options: Both numbers are classified as Sensitive Personal Information.
The Corporate ID is PI; the Passport Number is SPI.
Both numbers are classified as General Personal Information.
The Corporate ID is SPI; the Passport Number is Public Domain.
items.correct_answer: The Corporate ID is PI; the Passport Number is SPI.
items.explanation: SPI specifically includes numbers or licenses issued by government agencies peculiar to an individual. A private company ID does not meet this statutory definition and is PI.

items.question_text: A husband attempts to block a subpoena for confidential emails he sent his wife, claiming they are 'Privileged Information' under the DPA. Is this correct?
options: No, Privileged Information only applies to lawyers and doctors.
Yes, marital communications are protected under the Rules of Court.
No, digital emails cannot qualify for marital privilege under law.
Yes, but only if the emails contained highly sensitive financial data.
items.correct_answer: Yes, marital communications are protected under the Rules of Court.
items.explanation: Section 3(k) defines Privileged Information strictly via the Rules of Court. Because the Rules protect confidential marital communications, they are legally Privileged Information.

items.question_text: A dataset strips names but leaves Age, Zip Code, and a rare Diagnosis. Only one 34-year-old lives in that specific zip code. What is the classification?
options: It is legally Anonymized Data because explicit names were removed.
It is Sensitive Personal Information because the person is ascertainable.
It is Privileged Information because it originated from a diagnosis.
It is Public Domain Information because demographic stats are public.
items.correct_answer: It is Sensitive Personal Information because the person is ascertainable.
items.explanation: Anonymization fails if pseudo-identifiers are unique enough to single out a person. Because the identity can be reasonably ascertained, it remains Personal Information (and SPI).

items.question_text: A grocery app tracks standard food purchases and creates a hidden profile tag labeling a customer as 'Diabetic'. What is the classification of this tag?
options: General Personal Information, as it derives from grocery items.
Sensitive Personal Information, as it categorizes health conditions.
Trade Secret, as it is a proprietary corporate analytical inference.
Anonymized Data, provided the tag is stored in a separate database.
items.correct_answer: Sensitive Personal Information, as it categorizes health conditions.
items.explanation: Even if derived from non-sensitive data, an explicitly inferred tag regarding a specific medical condition constitutes health data, elevating it to Sensitive Personal Information.

items.question_text: A website's banner states: 'By continuing to scroll, you consent to data tracking.' A user scrolls to read an article. Is this valid consent?
options: Yes, the banner explicitly stated the specific conditions of navigation.
No, consent requires an affirmative act; implied consent is invalid.
Yes, but only for the first 24 hours of the user's browsing session.
No, because banners must be written in Tagalog to be legally binding.
items.correct_answer: No, consent requires an affirmative act; implied consent is invalid.
items.explanation: The DPA rejects 'implied consent' derived from silence or inaction. Scrolling is not a specific, affirmative indication of will, making the consent legally void.

items.question_text: A hospital collects biometrics solely for identity verification during admission. They later use this data to train a commercial AI. Is this lawful?
options: Yes, AI development is protected under the DPA research exemption.
No, training AI is an incompatible secondary purpose requiring consent.
Yes, provided the AI model remains strictly on hospital servers.
No, because biometrics can never be processed by machine learning.
items.correct_answer: No, training AI is an incompatible secondary purpose requiring consent.
items.explanation: Scope creep violates Legitimate Purpose. Repurposing verification biometrics to train a commercial AI model is fundamentally incompatible with the original declared purpose.

items.question_text: An executive keeps a disconnected hard drive containing old employee files in a vault for five years without plugging it in. Is this 'processing'?
options: No, processing legally requires active manipulation or viewing.
Yes, the statutory definition includes passive storage and holding.
No, data processing status expires after a three-year dormancy.
Yes, but only if the hard drive is eventually reconnected to power.
items.correct_answer: Yes, the statutory definition includes passive storage and holding.
items.explanation: The DPA defines processing exhaustively. Passive storage and holding of personal data, even offline, constitutes processing and is subject to security and retention rules.

items.question_text: A university shares its alumni list with an independent partner bank to offer credit cards. Both determine their own purposes. What document governs this?
options: A standard Outsourcing/Data Processing Agreement.
A formal Data Sharing Agreement (DSA) between independent PICs.
A unilateral Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) signed by the bank.
A Service Level Agreement (SLA) approved by the local government.
items.correct_answer: A formal Data Sharing Agreement (DSA) between independent PICs.
items.explanation: When two independent Personal Information Controllers share data for a new purpose, they must execute a Data Sharing Agreement, not an Outsourcing Agreement.

items.question_text: How can a company fulfill an erasure request for data stored on an immutable blockchain ledger where physical deletion is technically impossible?
options: By permanently destroying the cryptographic keys (crypto-shredding).
By simply ignoring the request, as blockchain is completely exempt.
By paying the user a financial settlement in digital cryptocurrency.
By requesting the NPC to physically shut down the local network nodes.
items.correct_answer: By permanently destroying the cryptographic keys (crypto-shredding).
items.explanation: When erasure is technologically impossible, regulators accept crypto-shredding. Destroying the decryption key renders the data permanently inaccessible, satisfying the erasure principle.

items.question_text: A breach exposes the basic PI of 70 individuals and the SPI of 35 different individuals (105 total). Does this trigger the 'large-scale' penalty?
options: No, because neither group independently reached the 100 threshold.
Yes, the law counts the aggregate total of affected data subjects.
No, large-scale penalties strictly require at least 1,000 subjects.
Yes, but the judge must issue separate sentences for the two groups.
items.correct_answer: Yes, the law counts the aggregate total of affected data subjects.
items.explanation: Section 35 dictates that a violation is large-scale if it affects 100 or more persons. The threshold is based on the aggregate total, regardless of the PI/SPI mix.

items.question_text: A corporate board pays a ransom to hackers to delete stolen SPI and intentionally files no breach reports to protect their stock price. What is the crime?
options: They are immune because paying the ransom mitigated the risk of harm.
Concealment of Security Breaches for suppressing the mandatory report.
Unauthorized Processing, because they communicated with hackers.
Improper Disposal, because they permitted hackers to delete the files.
items.correct_answer: Concealment of Security Breaches for suppressing the mandatory report.
items.explanation: Paying a ransom does not extinguish the statutory duty to report a qualifying breach. Intentionally hiding it from the NPC to avoid bad PR is a felony under Section 30.

items.question_text: An HR clerk uses the corporate database to send personalized fundraising emails for an orphanage, with zero malicious intent. Can they be criminally convicted?
options: No, the lack of criminal intent and charitable nature provide immunity.
Yes, DPA offenses are mala prohibita; the unauthorized act is the crime.
No, because registered charities are permanently exempt from the DPA.
Yes, but they can only be charged with Malicious Disclosure.
items.correct_answer: Yes, DPA offenses are mala prohibita; the unauthorized act is the crime.
items.explanation: Most DPA violations are mala prohibita. The intent behind the act is irrelevant; processing data for a completely unauthorized secondary purpose is a crime regardless of good faith.

items.question_text: An ex-employee posts highly accurate psychological evaluations of management on a revenge blog. In court, they argue the data is 100% true. Is this defense sound?
options: Yes, the constitutional protection of free speech covers verifiable facts.
No, truth is not a defense; Malicious Disclosure penalizes bad faith release.
Yes, Malicious Disclosure exclusively applies to fabricated personal data.
No, but the charge must be automatically downgraded to simple negligence.
items.correct_answer: No, truth is not a defense; Malicious Disclosure penalizes bad faith release.
items.explanation: Unlike libel, where truth can be a defense, Section 27 penalizes the malicious exposure of personal data. The accuracy of the data makes the privacy violation more damaging.

items.question_text: A hacker is charged with 'Illegal Access' under the Cybercrime Act and 'Unauthorized Processing' under the DPA. Does this violate Double Jeopardy?
options: Yes, an individual cannot be punished twice for one physical hack.
No, they penalize distinct legal elements and can proceed concurrently.
Yes, the Cybercrime Prevention Act automatically absorbs the DPA.
No, but the sentences must be served simultaneously in the same facility.
items.correct_answer: No, they penalize distinct legal elements and can proceed concurrently.
items.explanation: Double jeopardy does not apply when an act violates distinct statutes with different elements. The Cybercrime Act explicitly allows concurrent prosecution with other special laws.

items.question_text: A company requires the DPO to report to the Head of Marketing, who has the power to veto compliance audits. Why does this violate NPC guidelines?
options: Marketing departments are statutorily exempt from all DPA audits.
The DPO must have independence and report directly to top management.
The DPO can only report directly to the National Privacy Commission.
The DPO must hold an equal equity share in the corporate structure.
items.correct_answer: The DPO must have independence and report directly to top management.
items.explanation: To ensure objective oversight, the DPO must operate autonomously and report to the highest level of management (CEO/Board), preventing operational heads from suppressing findings.

items.question_text: A corporation outsources its DPO function to an external law firm. The firm misses a critical breach reporting deadline. Who is primarily accountable to the NPC?
options: The external law firm, as they contractually assumed all DPO liabilities.
The corporation (PIC), because statutory accountability cannot be delegated.
Both entities are fined exactly equal amounts under shared liability.
The DTI, for failing to properly accredit the outsourced DPO agency.
items.correct_answer: The corporation (PIC), because statutory accountability cannot be delegated.
items.explanation: While the physical duties of a DPO can be outsourced, the statutory accountability remains entirely with the PIC. The PIC is ultimately sanctioned by the NPC.

items.question_text: A DPO provides correct written advice to the Board regarding a patch. The Board ignores it to save money, resulting in a breach. Is the DPO criminally liable?
options: Yes, the DPO is strictly liable for any breach occurring under their watch.
No, the Board assumes liability; the DPO is an advisor, not the decision-maker.
Yes, but the DPO's penalty is automatically reduced by fifty percent.
No, because DPOs possess absolute diplomatic immunity from prosecution.
items.correct_answer: No, the Board assumes liability; the DPO is an advisor, not the decision-maker.
items.explanation: The DPO is an independent advisor. If they execute their duties properly but executive management (the responsible officers) ignores their advice, criminal liability falls on the executives.

items.question_text: A company designates its Head of IT Infrastructure, who designs all data flows, as the Data Protection Officer (DPO). Why does this violate Accountability?
options: The DPO must exclusively hold a background in legal compliance, not IT.
It creates a conflict of interest; they cannot objectively audit their own designs.
The Head of IT lacks the necessary seniority to communicate with the Board.
The DPO function must always be outsourced to a third-party audit firm.
items.correct_answer: It creates a conflict of interest; they cannot objectively audit their own designs.
items.explanation: An executive who controls the 'means' of processing (IT architecture) cannot objectively monitor and audit their own compliance, creating a fatal conflict of interest.

items.question_text: An organization encrypts its database using AES-256 but stores the decryption key in plaintext on the same server. Has the organization achieved the 'Encryption Safe Harbor'?
options: Yes, because AES-256 satisfies the highest technical standard for encryption.
No, improper key management renders the encryption ineffective, voiding the harbor.
Yes, provided the server itself is located in a physically secure facility.
No, safe harbor strictly requires the use of decentralized blockchain technology.
items.correct_answer: No, improper key management renders the encryption ineffective, voiding the harbor.
items.explanation: Encryption only provides a safe harbor if the data remains truly unintelligible. Storing the key alongside the ciphertext compromises the system, voiding the safe harbor.

items.question_text: A hospital uses advanced firewalls but allows nurses to leave patient charts openly on cafeteria tables. Which specific security pillar is failing?
options: Technical Security Measures.
Physical Security Measures.
Organizational Security Measures.
Environmental Security Measures.
items.correct_answer: Physical Security Measures.
items.explanation: Protecting manual filing systems and enforcing 'clean desk' policies to prevent unauthorized visual access to physical documents falls strictly under Physical Security Measures.

items.question_text: A bank installs biometric locks and advanced encryption but hires temporary contractors without conducting background checks to handle SPI. Which pillar failed?
options: Technical Security Measures.
Physical Security Measures.
Organizational Security Measures.
Systemic Security Measures.
items.correct_answer: Organizational Security Measures.
items.explanation: Organizational measures involve HR policies, privacy training, and background vetting. Allowing unvetted personnel to handle SPI is a severe organizational security failure.

items.question_text: A hospital database is highly encrypted, but all 500 nurses share a single generic login ('nurse_admin') to access it. Why does this violate Technical Security Measures?
options: Because passwords must be changed every 24 hours under DPA guidelines.
Because it destroys access control and accountability; individual auditing is impossible.
Because hospital databases must be kept completely offline without any logins.
It does not violate anything provided the password is highly complex and long.
items.correct_answer: Because it destroys access control and accountability; individual auditing is impossible.
items.explanation: Technical security requires robust access controls. Utilizing a shared generic login makes it technically impossible to track, audit, or hold specific individuals accountable.

items.question_text: An LGU plans to deploy a city-wide facial recognition CCTV network. Under the 5 Pillars of Compliance, what MUST be executed before deployment?
options: A comprehensive Financial Cost-Benefit Analysis.
A Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) to evaluate the high-risk processing of SPI.
A mandatory public referendum voted on by all city residents.
An immediate submission of the Annual Security Incident Report (ASIR).
items.correct_answer: A Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) to evaluate the high-risk processing of SPI.
items.explanation: Deploying high-risk, large-scale processing systems involving Sensitive Personal Information (biometrics) mandates the proactive execution of a documented Privacy Impact Assessment.

items.question_text: A startup writes a 2-page Privacy Notice for its website and claims they have completed their Privacy Management Program (PMP). Why is this incorrect?
options: A PMP must be at least 100 pages long to be legally valid in court.
A Privacy Notice is an external statement; a PMP is a comprehensive internal framework.
A PMP is only required for entities with over 1,000 employees.
The PMP must be physically signed by the National Privacy Commissioner.
items.correct_answer: A Privacy Notice is an external statement; a PMP is a comprehensive internal framework.
items.explanation: A Privacy Notice fulfills Transparency. A PMP is the holistic, internal organizational framework encompassing policies, risk assessments, and training that governs the enterprise.

items.question_text: At hour 71, a DPO experiences an internet outage. They print the breach report and have a courier deliver it physically to the NPC lobby. Is this compliant?
options: Yes, physical delivery with a timestamp represents the highest compliance standard.
No, the NPC mandates exclusive use of the DBNMS portal for breach submissions.
Yes, provided they email a digital PDF copy the following business day.
No, because motorcycle couriers are not legally authorized officers.
items.correct_answer: No, the NPC mandates exclusive use of the DBNMS portal for breach submissions.
items.explanation: The NPC established the Data Breach Notification Management System (DBNMS) as the exclusive, mandatory interface for submissions. Physical deliveries are procedurally non-compliant.

items.question_text: A registered corporation implements flawless security and experiences absolutely zero incidents or breaches all year. What must they file for their ASIR?
options: They are entirely exempt from filing an ASIR for that calendar year.
They must formally submit an ASIR declaring zero incidents via the DBNMS.
They only need to send a brief email to the NPC compliance desk.
They must undergo an expensive physical audit to verify the zero incidents.
items.correct_answer: They must formally submit an ASIR declaring zero incidents via the DBNMS.
items.explanation: The Annual Security Incident Report (ASIR) is a mandatory compliance requirement for registered entities. Even with a perfect record, they must formally file to declare zero incidents.

items.question_text: A DPO submits the preliminary report but realizes complex forensics will exceed the 5-day deadline for the Full Breach Report. What must they do?
options: Wait silently until forensics complete, then submit the massive final report.
Proactively submit a formal written request for an extension before the 5 days expire.
Retract the preliminary notification and entirely restart the 72-hour clock.
Submit the report to the Department of Information and Communications Technology.
items.correct_answer: Proactively submit a formal written request for an extension before the 5 days expire.
items.explanation: NPC Circular 16-03 strictly requires the Full Breach Report within 5 days. If impossible, the PIC must formally request an extension from the NPC before the deadline lapses.

items.question_text: Under NPC Circular 2022-04, which of the following automatically triggers mandatory registration of Data Processing Systems regardless of employee count?
options: Employing exactly 50 regular employees.
Processing the general personal information of 1,000 or more individuals.
Gross income exceeding PHP 10 Million.
Engaging in telecommunications, banking, or healthcare sectors.
items.correct_answer: Engaging in telecommunications, banking, or healthcare sectors.
items.explanation: Under Circular 2022-04, mandatory registration is triggered for entities operating in critical sectors (like telecommunications, banking, healthcare) regardless of their size.

items.question_text: The NBI verbally tells a DPO to delay notifying data subjects of a breach to protect a sting operation. Can the DPO lawfully delay notification based on this?
options: Yes, law enforcement orders automatically override NPC procedural rules.
No, the PIC must formally petition the NPC, who holds exclusive statutory authority.
Yes, provided the DPO writes an internal memo documenting the verbal request.
No, the 72-hour rule can never be delayed under any circumstance.
items.correct_answer: No, the PIC must formally petition the NPC, who holds exclusive statutory authority.
items.explanation: A PIC cannot unilaterally delay notification based on a police request. They must petition the NPC, which is the only authority that can grant a legal exemption or postponement.
